title: Happy Endings
full_review:
In terms of personal fulfillment, it's probably fair to say that everyone in Don Roos' film indeed gets their happy ending, but what happens beforehand is more problematic.

"Happy Endings" (Lions Gate) is an overly long and morally muddled mix of intertwining stories of the kind that Robert Altman or Paul Thomas Anderson would, frankly, do better. In its warts-and-all depiction of various characters, you're meant to empathize with their humanity, but the overall landscape is unrelievedly sordid.

Title cards interspersed throughout comment sardonically, but fail to add much in the way of real insight, amusing though some of them are.

First there's Mamie (Lisa Kudrow), currently involved with Mexican sex masseur Javier (Bobby Cannavale), with whom she acts out her sexual fantasies. Nicky (Jesse Bradford), a young would-be filmmaker, knows that Mamie once had a child whom she gave up for adoption. He'll reveal the boy's identity if Mamie allows him to film the reunion with her son, though this blackmail plan morphs into Nicky making a profile of Javier instead.

Mamie has a gay stepbrother, Charley (Steve Coogan), and it was he who sired her child when they were teenagers.

Now Charley worries that his companion, Gil (David Sutcliffe), is the father of the 2-year-old child of lesbian friends Diane (Sarah Clarke) and Pam (Laura Dern). Gil's sperm was once going to be used in artificial insemination but then they decided against it.

Charley obsesses about his theory until a threatened patrimony proceeding puts an end to the two couples' close friendship.

Then there's lounge singer Jude (Maggie Gyllenhaal), who seduces Otis (Jason Ritter), the sexually conflicted drummer son of a rich businessman (Tom Arnold), before casting an opportunistic eye on the older man.

You get the idea.

Roos, who made "The Opposite of Sex" and "Bounce," has turned out an edgy, offbeat comedy, and there are first-rate performances by Kudrow, Gyllenhaal and Arnold.

The script is not completely devoid of a moral center -- many of these dysfunctional people ultimately behave decently, and there's a subtext about the value of human life, including thoughtful discussions about abortion and its consequences -- but the results are just not profound or redemptive enough to overcome the general amorality on parade for most of the two hours-plus running time, thus precluding a recommendation.

The film contains profanity, crude language and expressions, abortion and artificial insemination, partial nudity, same-sex coupling, premarital and underage sex, drug use, sexual situations including brief partial nudity, and a violent car accident. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
